Characterising fish processing by-products                                                                                       2
Executive Summary
The objective of this project was to map both the capture fish processing supply
chain and the aquaculture fish processing supply chain in Scotland to understand
and characterise waste and by-products arising from fish handling and processing.
This report describes where and how different by-products and wastes arise as well
as the quantities, quality, consistency and current management routes. The focus of
the project was capture fisheries and aquaculture fish across Scotland. Excluded
from the scope of work were shellfish and aquaculture fish mortalities.
A total of 145 companies were identified from Seafood Scotland and Scottish
Seafood Association websites, with 49 of these considered to be of limited relevance
because of their size (information indicated that they were small-scale fishmongers or
traders). Aquaculture businesses which undertake primary processing (gutting) were
contacted through the Scottish Salmon Producers Organisation (SSPO) (now
Salmon Scotland) and other contacts. 96 companies (145 – 49) were therefore
contacted.
In terms of by-product arisings from primary, secondary and mixed processors,
Government sector reports were considered and compared with the survey data
secured.

Key findings for primary secondary and mixed processors
•   Aquaculture: It is estimated that there are 41,188 tonnes of aquaculture by-
    products being processed in Scotland each year, with the survey capturing
    information on 35,011 tonnes (85% of the total).
•   Capture fishing: An estimate has been made of 94,697 tonnes of by-products
    from capture fishing being processed in Scotland each year (using the sector
    reports). This assumes 50% of gutted capture fish are exported and 50% of the
    remainder are processed in the rest of the UK. The actual percentages for these
    movements is not currently understood/known. This survey has identified 32,946
    tonnes of by-products being produced by capture fish processors and
    subsequently processed in Scotland (35% of the estimated tonnage).


Key findings for by-products managed by added value processors
•   Inputs: 179,640 tonnes/year was identified from the survey, made up of 166,000
    tonnes of inputs to added value processors producing fishmeal and oil, with a
    further 13,640 tonnes input to processors drying or freezing by-products such as
    heads, frames, tails for human consumption, and selling these to higher value
    markets.
•   Outputs: The processing of the by-products removes mostly water with a total of
    56,528 tonnes of outputs/year, 49,800 tonnes of which are produced as a
    fishmeal and oil and 6,728 tonnes as dried/processed high value products.
•   The fishmeal and oils are ingredients for companies producing fish and
    agricultural feeds, depending on the source of the meal (e.g. salmon by-products



Characterising fish processing by-products                                             3
    cannot be processed and used as an ingredient for fish feeds destined for the
    salmon aquaculture sector).

Considering the above, the projected/estimated 135,885 tonnes of by-products
combined from aquaculture and capture fish processing (41,188 + 94,697) is 43,755
tonnes less than the total identified from the survey as inputs to the added value
processors in Scotland (see below). The reasons for this are unknown at this
moment in time. Assumptions have been made in terms of percentages for the
export of fish from Scotland and the rest of the UK (rUK), as well movements from
Scotland to the rUK for processing, and it is understood that actual data on such
movements is not readily available.

Conclusions
Key conclusions in terms of market prices, stability and seasonality are:
•   The companies engaged with in this survey were satisfied by the level of revenue
    that by-products from fish processing are generating. This ranged in value from
    £62 to £173 per tonne for mixed by-products and £250 to £520 per tonne for
    segregated products. None of the companies engaged with were being charged
    for the management of their by-products. The only charges identified were
    associated with the management of effluent/sludges and, in one case, food (non-
    fish) waste.
•   The survey identified that increased returns can be made from segregation and
    targeting specific by-products for specific markets.
•   None of the companies engaged with indicated that the current markets for their
    by-products were unstable or high risk. At the same time, the majority of by-
    products are being processed at only two sites on the Scottish mainland.
•   Although a number of companies identified seasonal impacts on their processing
    throughput associated with weather and natural fluctuations of different species,
    the majority of companies felt that seasonality was not a significant concern.
•   A significant number of companies are aware of the potential added value that
    they could secure by entering new and alternative markets. 60% (26 out of 43)
    companies that responded indicated that they were interested in developing their
    sites, with the markets of most interest being those associated with adding value
    to skins (4), developing ingredients for pharmaceutical products (4), developing
    infrastructure to maximise value from heads and frames (3), and developing
    products for other markets (3).

Recommendations
A number of recommendations have come from this project and survey:
•   A number of companies indicated interest in knowing more about how to develop
    their businesses to extract added value from by-products. In addition, several
    indicated that new business development and identifying how to reach new
    markets are not their strengths, and they would benefit greatly from and welcome
    support in these areas. It is recognised that there will be value in organisations
    such as Zero Waste Scotland, Scottish Enterprise and membership organisations

Characterising fish processing by-products                                              4
      such as Seafood Scotland, the Scottish Seafood Association and other key
      stakeholders considering the value of providing such support, and how it could
      most effectively be provided.
  •   The North East of Scotland and areas such as Peterhead have the potential to
      operate as centres of excellence for the fish processing sector, and there may be
      value in facilitating opportunities for different companies and support
      organisations to meet and discuss how the fish processing sector could be
      developed and supported generally. A key part of this would be to develop
      international reputation and for the fishing sector to widely view the region as
      such a centre of excellence, where maximum value is added and opportunities to
      maximise value exist.
  •   Although the companies engaged with indicated that they had no concerns
      regarding the stability of markets making use of their by-products, there may be
      value in considering sector support to develop higher value and alternative outlets
      to strengthen capacity and robustness in case of future fluctuations in prices.

1 Introduction
  The Scottish Government recognised in Scotland’s Circular Economy Strategy
  (Making Things Last1) that the food supply chain and the bioeconomy are significant
  opportunities in the move towards a circular economy. In particular, the fish industry
  has been identified as a key player.
  The Zero Waste Scotland Beer Whisky Fish report2 identified the tonnages of
  selected by-products available for valorisation across Scotland, and in 2018 a
  regional scan identifying the main circular economy opportunities in the North-east of
  Scotland estimated that around 61,000 tonnes of fish processing by-products are
  generated in the region each year. The majority of these by-products are sent for
  processing to fishmeal and oil with a smaller proportion dried to be exported.
  There is a strong will in the fish industry to explore and understand the potential of
  the circular economy for their sector. The sector is actively looking to enhance their
  sustainability credentials including through improved valorisation of all waste and by-
  products and Seafood Scotland have recently published Changing Tides, a Strategy
  for Scotland’s seafood industry3, which included an action to maximise the value of
  waste and by-products.

2 Objective
  The objective of this project was to map both the capture fish processing supply
  chain and the aquaculture fish processing supply chain in Scotland to understand
  and characterise waste and by-products arising from fish handling and processing.
  This project maps where and how different by-products and wastes arise as well as
  the quantities, quality, consistency and current management routes. The focus of the

  1 Scottish Government (2016). Making Things Last: a circular economy strategy for Scotland. [online]
  Scottish Government. [Accessed 3 Dec. 2024].
  2 Zero Waste Scotland (2015). Circular Economy Sector Study on Beer, Whisky and Fish Final Report
  2 Sector Study on Beer, Whisky and Fish. [online] Scottish Government. [Accessed 3 Dec. 2024].
  3 Seafood Scotland (2019). Changing Tides, a Strategy for Scotland’s seafood industry.

  Characterising fish processing by-products                                                         5
 project was capture seafish and aquaculture fish across Scotland. Excluded from the
 scope of work were shellfish and fish mortalities. The report also includes a review of
 the existing publications looking at mortalities4.
 This project was led by Zero Waste Scotland in partnership with a Fish By-products
 Stakeholder Group and has considered primary, secondary, mixed and added-value
 processors. The key questions addressed include:
 •   What is the process flow of material and processing practices?
 •   What are the raw feedstock materials and where are they sourced?
 •   What are the intended products and what tonnage/volume is currently processed?
 •   How much and what type of waste and by-products arise?
 •   What happens to waste and by-products and what separation or consolidation
     takes place?
 •   What is the cost or profit of materials being removed?
 •   What is its current and potential value, market and opportunities (on and off site)?
 •   Are there plans to expand or change current or future production processes and
     products?
 •   What are the perceived constraints and benefits of changing current practices?
 From an estimated 75 businesses involved in fish processing in Scotland, the aim
 was to target circa 35 companies through direct engagement/contacts to secure 25
 telephone interviews. Online surveys were set up targeting a 66% response rate. In
 addition, site visits were to be undertaken involving:
 •   At least one major primary fish processing facility
 •   At least one major fish by-product processing facility



3 Methodology
 The methodology for undertaking the project is described in the tasks listed below:
 •   Inception meeting – to discuss the project scope, programme and tasks to be
     delivered, and to consider ways in which Zero Waste Scotland and other
     stakeholders could support awareness raising and participation by the target
     companies e.g. by involving other stakeholders such as Seafood Scotland,
     Scottish Seafood Association (SSA) and Scottish Salmon Producers Organisation
     (SSPO) (now Salmon Scotland).
 •   Desk based research - to consider previous research/work and how this
     should/could influence the development of the approach to delivering the online
     survey and interviews.
 •   Survey and interview preparation - draft survey and interview questions reviewed
     by Zero Waste Scotland and Seafood Scotland.
 •   Online survey - prepare and publish final questions on SurveyMonkey and
     encourage participation.



 4 Zero Waste Scotland (2016). Finfish Mortalities in Scotland. [online] National Records of Scotland
 Web Archive. Zero Waste Scotland. [Accessed 3 Dec. 2024].

 Characterising fish processing by-products                                                             6
    •   Telephone surveys – carry out calls and encourage participation. These were
        lengthier than the online surveys involving more questions that required open
        responses from participating companies.
    •   Site visits - complete site visits with a sample of the interviewees.
    Emails were sent to members of Seafood Scotland, the Scottish Seafood Association
    (SSA) and the Scottish Salmon Producers Organisation (SSPO) with a description of
    the project, its objectives and links to the online survey. A project webpage was
    developed on the Enscape Consulting website with further information and a link to
    the online survey. In addition, the membership lists on the Seafood Scotland and
    SSA websites (freely available) were interrogated and a list of companies with
    contact names identified for telephone calls and emails.

 4 Desk-based review

4.1 Research in Scotland on fish processing arisings and potential
    valorisation
    The fish processing sector in Scotland has been described at an overarching level in
    recent years through the following two reports:
    •   Zero Waste Scotland, 2015, Sector Study on Beer, Whisky and Fish.
    •   Zero Waste Scotland, 2017, Biorefining Potential for Scotland.
    The 2015 Beer, Whisky and Fish report considered the sector and provided indicative
    inputs and outputs, including consideration of aquaculture, capture fishing, shellfish,
    aquaculture mortalities and non-quota species. The outputs were described as
    160,250 tonnes of fish processing waste and 24,000 tonnes of shellfish waste.
    The 2017 Biorefining Report referred to fish processing waste and for the purposes
    of its model provided an estimated split of the 160,250 tonnes above, and split this
    into the following categories to demonstrate the potential to the sector:
    •   Skin: 5%, 8,013 tonnes
    •   Trimmings (not defined): 55%, 88,138 tonnes
    •   Bones: 20%, 32,050 tonnes
    •   Viscera: 20%, 32,050 tonnes
    The report referred to aquaculture fish by-product feedstock material arisings of
    2,811 tonnes but did not provide any further information (or definition) for this.

4.2 Government research carried out on fish mortalities in Scotland
    Aquaculture fish mortalities were excluded from the scope of the survey; however,
    the status of the sector is summarised here. The intention in doing so is to provide
    an indication of the tonnages arising and seasonality in case these may assist
    companies considering an investment in new infrastructure for the processing of fish
    waste or by-products. A more viable opportunity may arise from considering how
    mortalities and by-products could be managed at one site with some shared
    infrastructure (e.g. buildings, supply of heat and power, etc). However, it should be
    noted that fish mortalities are usually described as Category 2 animal by-product


    Characterising fish processing by-products                                              7
    wastes5 and, therefore, depending on the business model, need to be handled
    separately and differently to by-products from fish processing (which are Category 3
    by-products). The Scottish Government has produced reports in recent years which
    characterise the quantity, geographical distribution and seasonality associated with
    fish mortalities from the aquaculture sector with a particular emphasis on salmon.
    These reports are:
    •   2016, Fish mortalities in Scotland6
    •   2018, Contingency planning for fish mortalities in Scotland7
    The 2018 report indicated that there was a total of 25,737 tonnes of salmon
    mortalities in 2017 and that the majority of these occurred, historically, in the period
    September to November.

4.3 Using government and industry data to indicate flows of products, wastes
    and by-products
    The Scottish Government annually produces two reports which indicate the quantity
    of aquaculture and capture fish landed in Scotland. These reports (indicated below)
    were used to inform the extent to which the data captured in this survey of fish
    processors describes behaviour in Scotland.

    •   Scottish Fish Farm Production Survey (latest version, 2018)
    •   Scottish Sea Fisheries Statistics (latest version, 2018)

    In Figure 1, a tonnage of 198,903 is shown for aquaculture Whole Fish Equivalent
    (WFE) based on the projected figure for 2019 (in the 2018 Production Survey). The
    figure provides an indicative flow and estimate of how fish may then be subsequently
    processed to assist with understanding how much of the total by-products generated
    in Scotland have been identified by the survey. For example, head-on-gutted (HOG)
    fish is often exported directly out of Scotland and the rest of the UK (rUK), and then a
    further percentage of the remaining HOG fish is shipped out of Scotland to the rUK
    for processing. Other by-products generated in Scotland are then also sent to the
    rUK for processing. These flows of product and by-products significantly impact on
    the tonnage of by-products (heads, trimmings, bone, skin) available for processing in
    Scotland.

    Figure 2 shows a similar flowchart for capture fishing (pelagic and demersal),
    however, there is much greater uncertainty in terms of the flow of fish out of
    Scotland, and it is understood that this information may not currently be collated in a
    form that allows the flowchart to be populated with percentages and tonnages with
    any kind of certainty. Question marks (?) are shown in the places where this is the
    case. Where possible, both flowcharts show (in red font) the estimated tonnage of

by-products generated and available for processing in Scotland. This is described
as:
•   Aquaculture estimate (Figure 1): 41,188 tonnes (17,901 guts + 23,287 other)
•   Capture fishing estimate (Figure 2): not made (22,396 guts + ? other tonnes)




Figure 1. Flowchart showing supply chain movements of harvested aquaculture fish

Description of figure 1
The flowchart starts with 198,903 tonnes of Whole Fish Equivalent (WFE), all of
which are gutted in Scotland. From here, the flow splits into two categories: 91% of
the weight and 9% of the weight.
The 9% portion, equating to 17,901 tonnes, consists of guts and blood, all processed
in Scotland. The remaining 91% is divided further. One part, representing 45% of the
total WFE weight (81,451 tonnes), is exported from Scotland and the wider UK as
Head-On Gutted (HOG) fish. The other part, 55% of the WFE weight (99,551 tonnes),
is retained within Scotland and the rest of the UK for further processing.
Of the 99,551 tonnes retained, 24,888 tonnes (25%) are sent to the rest of the UK for
processing, while 74,663 tonnes (75%) are processed within Scotland. The portion
sent to the rest of the UK for processing is further split into products and by-products.
Similarly, of the 74,663 tonnes processed in Scotland, 23,287 tonnes are converted
to products (76% of by-product arisings), while the remaining 24% is categorised as
by-products and sent to the rest of the UK for further processing.



Characterising fish processing by-products                                              9
The total aquaculture by-products processed in Scotland equals 41,188 tonnes
(17,901 tonnes of guts plus 23,287 of other).




Figure 2. Flowchart showing supply chain movements of capture fish (demersal and pelagic)

Description of figure 2
The flowchart starts with 155,305 tonnes of pelagic and 150,070 tonnes of demersal
(gutted) fish, all of which are gutted in Scotland. The flow indicates that 100% of
pelagic fish are gutted on land. From here, the flow splits into two categories: 88% of
the weight and 12% of the weight.
The 12% portion, equating to 22,396 tonnes, consists of guts and blood, all
processed in Scotland. The remaining 88% (282,079 tonnes) consisting of gutted fish
is divided further, however, there is a large degree of uncertainty in terms of the flow
of fish out of Scotland so the flowchart cannot be populated with percentages and
tonnages beyond this point. One branch is exported from Scotland and the wider UK
as gutted fish. The other part is retained within Scotland and the rest of the UK for
further processing.
From here the chart splits, with one branch showing the gutted fish being processed
into by-products and products in Scotland, and the other showing the gutted fish
being processed into by-products and products in the rest of the UK.
It is not possible to estimate the total capture fish by-products processed in Scotland
with the large degree of uncertainty in the data.

 5 Survey results

5.1 Overview
   This summary report provides an overview of the main findings from the survey, with
   detailed tables and results (with some analysis, assumptions stated, etc) provided in
   Appendix A. The questions used for the survey are shown in Appendix B.
   A total of 145 companies were identified from Seafood Scotland and Scottish
   Seafood Association websites, with 49 of these considered to be of limited relevance
   because of their size (information indicated that they were small-scale fishmongers or
   traders). Aquaculture businesses which undertake primary processing (gutting) were
   contacted through the SSPO and other contacts. 96 companies (145 – 49) were
   therefore contacted and surveys completed by 53 of these - 39 of which were
   through telephone interviews and 14 from online surveys. This meant the following:
   •   37% of the 145 companies identified (including smaller fishmongers / traders)
       completed surveys.
   •   55% of the 96 companies identified (excluding smaller fishmongers / traders)
       completed surveys.
   The number of online survey responses were significantly lower than the targeted
   response rate. To compensate for this a far higher level of engagement took place
   through telephone calls, interviews and follow ups (including emails). Two site visits
   were undertaken: one mixed processing (primary and secondary) facility and one
   added value (by-product) processor.
   A breakdown of the types of processors responding to the survey is provided in Table
   1.

The structure of fish harvested, captured and processed is considered in this report
based on the flow summarised in Figure 3.




Characterising fish processing by-products                                             12
Figure 3. Flowchart of fish harvesting and processing stages




Characterising fish processing by-products                     13
    Description of figure 3
    The flowchart starts with two branches. The first is aquaculture fish which flows to
    fish landed in Scotland (quayside) before flowing to primary processing. The other
    branch starts with capture fishing – pelagic and demersal species which splits into
    guts/organs discard to sea and fish landed in Scotland (ports). Fish landed in
    Scotland (ports) then splits, with one branch leading to exported and the other
    flowing in primary processing.
    Primary processing is split into three sections. They are exported, guts, and a larger
    group of by-products comprised of main products: fillets, cheeks, tongues, etc.,
    heads, frames and tails, skins, guts (from some pelagic and smaller fish), trimmings,
    and rejects. The larger group of by-products are split out further.
    Main products: fillets, cheeks, tongues, etc. Splits into secondary processing (e.g.
    Smoking) and domestic and export sales. Heads, frames and tails, Skins, guts (from
    some pelagic and smaller fish), trimmings, and rejects flow to added value (by-
    product) processing involving cooking, separating, evaporation, which ends in either
    oil or meal. Heads also splits into added value (by-product) processing involving
    drying or freezing, then Export sales.
    The flowchart includes three notes. Firstly, that approximately 45-50% of gutted fish
    comprise by-products (heads, tails/frames, skin). Secondly, by-product conversion to
    oil and meal is approximately 5-10% oil, 20% meal, 70 to 75% water losses. Finally,
    drying of fish heads/frames produces approximately 20% dried products, 80% water
    losses.

Characterising fish processing by-products                                                                                                                           21
Description of figure 8
The flowchart presents survey data, starting with 179,640 tonnes of by-products to added value processors which then flows to
56,528 tonnes of products from added value (and 123,112 tonnes of water/steam effluent).
By-products to added value processors is split into mixed (166,000 tonnes) and segregated (13,640 tonnes) by-products.
The mixed by-products are comprised of 18,220 tonnes from aquaculture, 11,063 tonnes from capture fishing, and 136,717
tonnes of material not identified by the survey. This then flows to ingredients for 3rd party products (49,800 tonnes) which is
further broken down into meal (28,200 tonnes), oil (14,100 tonnes) and premium animal feed, oil, protein (7,500). This then flows
to 49,800 tonnes of final product including fish feed, agricultural feed, and others.
The segregated by-products are comprised of 3,000 tonnes of heads, 2,000 tonnes of tails, and 8,640 tonnes of heads and
frames. This then flows to high value products, including for human consumption (6,728 tonnes) which is further broken down
into heads and frames (5,728 tonnes), heads (600 tonnes), and frames (400 tonnes).




Characterising fish processing by-products                                                                                      22
    The following is a summary of the data provided in the previous flowcharts:
    Figure 5 and Figure 6: By-product arisings from primary, secondary and mixed
    processors – projected from government sector reports and compared with the
    survey data
    •   Aquaculture: It is estimated that there are 41,188 tonnes of aquaculture by-
        products being processed in Scotland, with the survey capturing information on
        35,011 tonnes (85% of the total).
    •   Capture Fishing: An estimate/projection has been made of 94,697 tonnes of by-
        products from capture fishing being processed in Scotland. This is based on 50%
        of gutted capture fish being exported and 50% of the remainder being processed
        in the rUK. The actual percentages for these movements is not currently
        understood/known. The survey has identified 32,946 tonnes of by-products being
        produced by fish processors and subsequently processed in Scotland (35% of the
        estimate).
    •   Comparison with the inputs to Added Value Processors: The projected/estimated
        135,885 tonnes of by-products combined from aquaculture and capture fishing is
        43,755 tonnes less than the total identified as being processed by the Added
        Value processors in Scotland (see discussion points below). The survey
        identified a combined total of 67,956 tonnes of by-products from aquaculture and
        capture fishing, which is 50% of the estimated/projected arisings (using the
        assumptions stated above).

    Figure 8, Added value processing inputs and outputs
    •   Inputs: 179,640 tonnes was identified from the survey, made up of 166,000
        tonnes of inputs to added value processors producing fishmeal and oil, with a
        further 13,640 tonnes input to processors drying/freezing by-products such as
        heads, frames, tails for human consumption, and therefore, selling these to higher
        value markets.
    •   Outputs: The processing of the by-products removes mostly water with a total of
        56,528 tonnes of outputs, 49,800 tonnes of which are produced as a fishmeal and
        oil and 6,728 tonnes as dried/processed high value products.
    •   The fishmeal and oils are ingredients for companies producing fish and
        agricultural feeds, depending on the source of the fishmeal (e.g. salmon by-
        products cannot be processed and used as an ingredient for fish feeds destined
        for the salmon aquaculture sector).


5.4 Seasonality impacts
    In terms of seasonality, there were 25 responses from fish processors, with 48% (12)
    of these indicating that there was “some” variability across the year, and 32% (8)
    indicating that their throughput was consistent (often the seasonality with one species
    would be compensated for by another species, or on some occasions by shellfish).
    However, for those indicating that there was a significant variation (20%, 5

    Characterising fish processing by-products                                           23
    respondents) this was mostly related to species seasons and weather (12 of the 17
    responses). These results are summarised in Table 3 and Table 4 below.

    Q. Would there be variability in processing throughput across the year e.g. seasonal
    impacts?

        year e.g. varies less                           variability
        than 10%

        32%                     48%                     20%

5.5 Costs and incomes from by-products
    None of the companies engaged with were incurring a cost for the management of
    their solid by-products generated from fish processing. A number of companies did
    highlight that the management of their sludges/effluent did incur a cost, however, this
    was not gone into in any further depth as this was outwith the scope of this project.

    In terms of the income streams generated, there were no examples of companies
    indicating that the value they were generating from the sale of by-products was a
    cause for concern. This was generally considered positively by the sector.
    Information on the actual values secured in 2019 is provided in Table 5 and Table 6
    below. The tables provide:

    •   Range of average £/tonne income: where companies provided a range of prices
        an average of the low and high £/tonne prices is stated.



    Characterising fish processing by-products                                               24
    •   Average of exact £ Income/tonne: where companies provided a specific price, an
        average of this, £/tonne is stated.

    The above is provided for both mixed by-products and segregated by-products
    produced by processors. No evidence was found from the survey that companies
    producing by-products were being charged for the management of these.

    Q. Could you indicate below which wastes and by-products generate an income, and
    provide an estimate of the overall income for these last year (2019)?

    The prices stated above may not be the maximum rate being earned for certain by-
    products, with a number of companies not divulging this information. It should be
    noted that prices offered for by-products to be sold as food (e.g. fish heads bought
    for drying and onward sale) were significantly higher than those sold for rendering
    into fishmeal and oil.

5.6 Market stability
    None of the companies engaged with identified that there were high risks associated
    with the stability of markets taking their by-products, as summarised in Table 7
    below. In general, companies have indicated that they are content with the service
    provided and the prices paid, which they have indicated have remained steady over a
    significant period of time. However, there may be a different outcome to this question
    if the prices paid for by-products were to significantly drop.

5.7 Business development opportunities and constraints
    Companies were asked about added-value markets. When asked about market
    awareness, 27 responded that they were aware of the potential for added value for
    their by-products, and 1 company indicated that it was sceptical of such markets.

    When asked if they were interested in developing their sites to enable them to
    process/manage by-products for higher value markets, 19 commented that they were
    interested in doing so (Table 8), with a wide spread in terms of the options for doing
    so. This included:

        •    adding value to skins
        •    developing ingredients for pharmaceutical products
        •    developing infrastructure to maximise value from heads and frames
        •    developing products for other human markets
        •    producing their own meal and oil
        •    pursuing international sales
        •    processing meat from frames
        •    processing Haddock cheeks
        •    pursuing CAT2 markets

    Those companies that provided a qualified interest (“yes, but depends”) provided
    reasons, these being:

    •   Need more tonnage
    •   Need support
    •   Location (constraints) make this difficult
    •   Need for knowledge, contacts to develop the markets.




    Characterising fish processing by-products                                            26
  Q. Are you interested in developing sites for higher value markets?

    Yes           No           A little     Difficult     Yes, but    TOTAL
                                                          depends …

    19            13           1            3             7           43

    44.2%         30.2%        2.3%         7.0%          16.3%
  Table 8. Interest in developing sites for higher value market


6 Conclusions
  An estimate was made of the potential quantity of by-products processed in Scotland
  by considering Scottish Government sector reports for both the aquaculture and
  capture fishing sectors. This amounted to 41,278 tonnes of by-products for the
  former and 94,697 tonnes for the latter (a total of 135,885 tonnes).

  The company survey identified 35,011 tonnes from aquaculture processing and
  32,946 tonnes from capture fish processing – a total of 67,956 tonnes (50% of the
  estimate).

  The engagement with added value processors, taking by-products from primary and
  secondary processors (and mixed processors) identified that they were accepting a
  total of 179,640 tonnes, and after processing (drying/separation) putting out a total of
  59,120 tonnes to markets.

  The reason for a difference in the projected/estimated by-products processed in
  Scotland compared to the quantity identified in the survey is unknown. Assumptions
  have been made in terms of percentages for the export of fish from Scotland and the
  rUK, as well movements from Scotland to the rUK for processing, and it is
  understood that actual data on such movements is not readily available.

  The companies engaged with in this survey were satisfied by the level of revenue
  that by-products from fish processing are generating. This ranged in value from £62
  to £173 per tonne for mixed by-products and £250 to £520 per tonne for segregated
  products. None of the companies engaged with were being charged for the
  management of their by-products. The only charges identified were associated with
  the management of effluent/sludges and in one case food (non-fish) waste.

  The survey has identified that increased returns can be made from segregation and
  targeting specific by-products for specific markets.

  None of the companies engaged indicated that the current markets for their by-
  products were unstable or high risk. At the same time the majority of by-products are
  being processed at only two sites on the Scottish mainland.



  Characterising fish processing by-products                                            27
    Although a number of companies did identify that there were seasonal impacts on
    their processing throughput associated with weather and the natural fluctuations of
    different species, the majority of companies felt that seasonal impacts were not a
    significant concern.

    A significant number of companies are aware of the potential added value that they
    could secure by entering new and alternative markets. 60% (26 out of 43) of
    companies that responded indicated that they were interested in developing their
    sites, with the markets of interest being, for example, those associated with adding
    value to skins, developing ingredients for pharmaceutical products, developing
    infrastructure to maximise value from heads and frames, and developing products for
    other human markets.


 7 Recommendations
    A number of companies have indicated that they are interested in knowing more
    about how to develop their businesses to extract added value from by-products. A
    number have indicated that new business development and identifying how to reach
    new markets are not their strengths, and they would benefit greatly from support in
    these areas. There may be value in organisations such as Zero Waste Scotland,
    Scottish Enterprise and membership organisations such as Seafood Scotland, the
    Scottish Seafood Association and other key stakeholders considering the value of
    providing such support, and how it could most effectively be provided.

    The Northeast of Scotland and areas such as Peterhead have the potential to
    operate as centres of excellence for the fish processing sector, and there may be
    value in facilitating opportunities for different companies and support organisations to
    meet and discuss how the fish processing sector could be developed and supported
    generally. A key part of this would be to develop international reputation and for the
    fishing sector to widely view the region as such a centre of excellence, where
    maximum value is added and opportunities to maximise value exist.

    Although the companies engaged indicated that they had no concerns regarding the
    stability of markets taking their by-products, there may be value in considering if the
    sector could be supported to develop higher value and alternative outlets to
    strengthen capacity and robustness in case of future fluctuations in prices.



    Glossary of terms

Term                  Definition

Added value           Processors of fish by-products e.g. drying heads, frames, manufacturing
processors            oils and concentrates etc.


    Characterising fish processing by-products                                            28
Animal by-products     Animal by-products are materials of animal origin that people do not
(ABPs)                 consume.

Aquaculture            The cultivation and farming of fish under controlled conditions.

By-products            The parts of fish remaining after fillets from primary, secondary and mixed
                       processing have been produced.

Capture fishing        Fishing of pelagic and/or demersal fish.

Demersal fish          Fish that live and feed on or near the bottom of seas or lochs.

Head-on-gutted         Fish after the removal of viscera.
(HOG)

Mixed processors       Organisations carrying out both primary and secondary processing

Pelagic fish           Fish that live in the pelagic zone of ocean or loch waters, neither close to
                       the bottom or near the shore.

Primary processors     Organisations cutting, peeling, gutting and washing fish

Scottish Salmon        A member organisation for Scotland’s salmon farming industry, with the
Producers              aim of giving the industry a voice and promoting best practice. They
Organisation           changed their name in 2021 to Salmon Scotland.
(SSPO)

Seafood Scotland       A national trade and marketing body for the Scottish seafood industry.

Scottish Sea food      A national representative body for Scottish seafood processors.
Association (SSA)

Secondary              Organisations brining, smoking, freezing, canning and the manufacture of
processors             fish products such as fishcakes, breaded fillets and packaged meals

Whole fish             This is a standard weight definition for fish after gutting.
equivalent (WFE)
